clips.title: The Human Is an Async API — Melanie Warrick, Temporal
clips.why: Melanie Warrick from Temporal explains why an agent must never block while it waits for a person, and the two tools that solve it: a wait condition and a signal.
look: Why a blocking call fails: a person may answer in a minute or in three days.
The pair she shows, a wait condition plus a signal, is our condition plus decidePlan.
clips.after: Our plan approval is exactly this pattern, with a timeout added so Nova can remind you and park the ticket.

clips.title: Temporal Live Coding Demo: Handling Failures & Human Interaction
clips.why: A live demo of a timer racing a signal: whichever comes first decides what the workflow does next.
look: The timer and the signal are both waited for at the same time. That is condition with a timeout.
Notice what decides the next step: the timer firing first, or the person acting first.
clips.after: In waitForPerson the person races two timers: the reminder after one day and parking after three.

clips.title: The Human Is an Async API — Melanie Warrick, Temporal
clips.why: In the second demo a high-value order needs a person, and she kills the worker while it waits for the approval.
look: The order waits for a person, and no code runs during the wait.
After the worker is killed and started again, the run continues with the approval that arrived.
clips.after: It is the same as the lab's outage step: your approval is kept by Temporal and delivered when a worker comes back.

practice.q: Which tool fits this need? You want Nova to start building the moment the requester presses Approve.

options.text: A signal that sets decision, and condition(() => decision !== undefined, timeout)
options.why: The signal records the click, and condition continues as soon as the decision is set, with the timeout as the deadline.

options.text: A query that the Slack app calls when the button is pressed
options.why: A query only reads. It cannot change the run, so it cannot deliver a decision.

options.text: A loop in the workflow that sleeps one minute and checks Jira
options.why: That adds a timer to the history every minute and reacts up to a minute late. A signal reaches the run directly.

practice.q: Finish the wait: true if a decision arrives within a day, false if the day passes first.
practice.hint: It comes from @temporalio/workflow and waits until a function returns true.
practice.why: condition with a timeout returns a boolean, so the workflow knows whether the person acted or the time ran out.

practice.q: Attach the handler so the decision from the button is stored when the signal arrives.
practice.hint: The same function attaches signal handlers and query handlers.
practice.why: setHandler connects a defined signal to a small function in the workflow. Set it at the top, before the first await.

practice.q: Nobody presses anything on RH-1234's plan. Put what happens in order.
items: Nova posts the plan, and the workflow calls condition with a one-day timeout
One day passes, the timer fires and condition returns false
Nova reminds the requester in the Slack thread and on Jira
The workflow waits again, this time for two days
The second timer fires, the ticket goes back to the requester, and the run ends as parked
practice.why: Two durable timers carry the whole wait. No VM runs and no code runs between the steps.

practice.q: The workers are being deployed for one minute. Which of these still works during that minute?

options.text: /nova status RH-1234, which sends the status query
options.why: A query is computed by a worker. With no worker running it waits and then fails.

options.text: Pressing Approve, which sends the decidePlan signal
options.why: The Temporal Service records the signal at once. The next worker delivers it to the handler.

options.text: Neither: Slack shows an error for both
options.why: Only the query needs a worker. Signals were designed to survive exactly this.
